name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q01 - Decomposition steps and their defining mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Match the decomposition processes in List-I with their corresponding mechanisms in List-II:

List-I (Process) List-II (Mechanism)
A. Fragmentation I. Water-soluble inorganic nutrients precipitate into the soil horizon as unavailable salts
B. Leaching II. Degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes
C. Catabolism III. Breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores
D. Humification IV. Accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous colloidal substance resistant to microbial action

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand physical breakdown by detritivores.
Detritivores, such as earthworms, break down detritus into smaller particles. This mechanical process is defined as fragmentation.

Step 2: Understand the percolation of soluble nutrients.
During leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients move downward into the soil horizon and precipitate as unavailable salts.

Step 3: Understand enzymatic degradation by microbes.
Catabolism is the process where extracellular bacterial and fungal enzymes chemically degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.

Step 4: Understand the accumulation of humus.
Humification leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial degradation and serves as a nutrient reservoir.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Fragmentation matches breakdown of detritus into smaller particles; Leaching matches precipitation of water-soluble inorganic nutrients into the soil horizon; Catabolism matches enzymatic degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances; and Humification matches accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance resistant to microbial action.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q02 - Pond ecosystem components and representative examples

questiontext.text:
Match the pond ecosystem functional components in List-I with their corresponding representatives in List-II:

List-I (Pond Component) List-II (Representative Group)
A. Autotrophic components I. Zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms
B. Consumers II. Phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants
C. Decomposers III. Water with dissolved inorganic substances and rich bottom soil deposit
D. Abiotic components IV. Fungi, bacteria and flagellates abundant at the pond bottom

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify autotrophic components in a pond.
Autotrophs convert radiant solar energy into organic materials; in a pond, they are represented by phytoplankton, algae, and floating, submerged, or marginal plants.

Step 2: Identify heterotrophic consumers in a pond.
Consumers feed directly or indirectly on autotrophs; in a pond, these include zooplankton, along with free-swimming and benthic (bottom-dwelling) animals.

Step 3: Identify decomposers in an aquatic habitat.
Decomposers break down dead organic matter and mineralise it; in a pond, these are saprotrophic fungi, bacteria, and flagellates concentrated at the pond bottom.

Step 4: Identify the physical and chemical abiotic environment.
The abiotic matrix consists of water with its dissolved organic and inorganic materials, alongside the mineral-rich soil deposited at the pond bottom.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Autotrophic components match phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants; Consumers match zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; Decomposers match fungi, bacteria and flagellates; and Abiotic components match water with dissolved inorganic substances and bottom soil deposit.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q03 - Ecosystem productivity definitions and biosphere values

questiontext.text:
Match the productivity terms in List-I with their corresponding definitions or annual values in List-II:

List-I (Productivity Term) List-II (Definition / Biosphere Value)
A. Gross primary productivity I. Rate of synthesis of new organic matter by consumers
B. Net primary productivity II. Total rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
C. Secondary productivity III. Approximately 55 billion tons dry weight despite covering 70% of Earth's surface
D. Annual oceanic productivity IV. Biomass available for consumption by herbivores and decomposers after respiratory losses

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define gross primary productivity.
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate at which organic matter or biomass is produced by autotrophs through photosynthesis per unit area over a specified time.

Step 2: Define net primary productivity.
Net primary productivity (NPP) is gross primary productivity minus respiration losses (\(\text{GPP} - R = \text{NPP}\)). It represents the organic biomass remaining and available for consumption by heterotrophic herbivores and decomposers.

Step 3: Define secondary productivity.
Secondary productivity represents the assimilation and generation of new organic biomass specifically carried out by consumers.

Step 4: Analyze annual ocean productivity.
Although oceans occupy roughly 70 percent of the Earth's surface, their total annual net primary productivity is only about 55 billion tons (dry weight) out of the global 170 billion tons.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Gross primary productivity matches the total rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis; Net primary productivity matches the biomass available for consumption by herbivores and decomposers after respiratory losses; Secondary productivity matches the rate of synthesis of new organic matter by consumers; and Annual oceanic productivity matches approximately 55 billion tons dry weight.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q04 - Trophic levels and representative member organisms

questiontext.text:
Match the trophic levels in List-I with their typical representative organisms in List-II:

List-I (Trophic Level) List-II (Representative Organisms)
A. First trophic level I. Birds, fishes, wolf
B. Second trophic level II. Man, lion
C. Third trophic level III. Phytoplankton, grass, trees
D. Fourth trophic level IV. Zooplankton, grasshopper, cow

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify organisms of the first trophic level.
The first trophic level consists of primary producers or autotrophs that fix radiant energy into food; examples include phytoplankton in aquatic ecosystems and grass or trees in terrestrial ecosystems.

Step 2: Identify organisms of the second trophic level.
The second trophic level consists of primary consumers (herbivores) feeding directly on autotrophs; examples include zooplankton, grasshoppers, and cows.

Step 3: Identify organisms of the third trophic level.
The third trophic level comprises secondary consumers (primary carnivores) feeding on herbivores; examples include birds, carnivorous fishes, and wolves.

Step 4: Identify organisms of the fourth trophic level.
The fourth trophic level contains tertiary consumers (top carnivores) that feed on secondary consumers; examples include top predators such as lion and man.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
First trophic level matches phytoplankton, grass, trees; Second trophic level matches zooplankton, grasshopper, cow; Third trophic level matches birds, fishes, wolf; and Fourth trophic level matches man, lion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q05 - Detritus composition and climatic decomposition factors

questiontext.text:
Match the detritus chemical nature or climatic condition in List-I with its effect on decomposition in List-II:

List-I (Detritus / Climatic Condition) List-II (Effect on Rate of Decomposition)
A. Detritus rich in lignin and chitin I. Decomposition rate is markedly slower
B. Detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars II. Decomposition rate is significantly quicker
C. Warm and moist environment III. Favours microbial activity and promotes rapid breakdown
D. Low temperature and anaerobiosis IV. Inhibits decomposition resulting in the build-up of organic materials

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate structural refractory compounds.
Lignin and chitin are complex structural polymers that resist enzymatic degradation; detritus rich in these substances undergoes breakdown at a noticeably slower rate.

Step 2: Evaluate readily metabolised chemical compounds.
Substances containing high levels of nitrogen and soluble carbohydrates like sugars provide easily accessible energy and nutrients to decomposers, resulting in quicker decomposition.

Step 3: Analyze optimal climatic factors.
Microbial metabolism accelerates under warm temperatures and optimal moisture, making warm and moist conditions highly favourable for decomposition.

Step 4: Analyze inhibitory conditions.
Low temperatures drastically slow down microbial enzymatic activity, and oxygen deficiency (anaerobiosis) arrests oxidative catabolism; together, they inhibit decomposition, leading to an accumulation of undecomposed organic matter.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Detritus rich in lignin and chitin matches slower decomposition rate; Detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars matches quicker decomposition rate; Warm and moist environment matches favouring microbial activity and rapid breakdown; and Low temperature and anaerobiosis matches inhibiting decomposition and causing build-up of organic materials.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q06 - Ecological pyramid types and ecosystem characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match the ecological pyramids in List-I with their characteristic features in List-II:

List-I (Pyramid Type) List-II (Characteristic Shape / Feature)
A. Pyramid of numbers in a grassland I. Upright, with standing biomass sharply decreasing at each successive trophic step
B. Pyramid of biomass in a forest II. Inverted, because the standing crop of primary producers is far exceeded by consumers
C. Pyramid of biomass in an ocean III. Upright, millions of autotrophs support only a very small number of top carnivores
D. Pyramid of energy IV. Always upright, can never be inverted due to progressive dissipative heat loss

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand grassland number pyramids.
In a grassland, nearly six million primary producers (grasses) form a broad base that supports primary and secondary consumers, terminating in only three top carnivores, forming an upright pyramid.

Step 2: Understand forest biomass pyramids.
In a terrestrial forest ecosystem, large woody autotrophs contribute massive standing dry biomass, which progressively declines across herbivores and carnivores, producing an upright pyramid of biomass.

Step 3: Understand oceanic biomass pyramids.
In open oceans, phytoplankton possess high turnover rates but very small instantaneous standing crop, which supports a much larger standing biomass of long-lived zooplankton and fishes, creating an inverted biomass pyramid.

Step 4: Understand the thermodynamic law governing energy pyramids.
In compliance with the second law of thermodynamics, energy transfers between trophic levels are accompanied by dissipative heat loss, ensuring that available energy decreases at higher levels and making the pyramid of energy strictly upright in all ecosystems.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Pyramid of numbers in a grassland matches upright where millions of autotrophs support only a few top carnivores; Pyramid of biomass in a forest matches upright with standing biomass sharply decreasing at successive steps; Pyramid of biomass in an ocean matches inverted because standing crop of producers is exceeded by consumers; and Pyramid of energy matches always upright and can never be inverted.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q07 - Energy flow conduits and trophic chain attributes

questiontext.text:
Match the food chain conduits and properties in List-I with their corresponding descriptions in List-II:

List-I (Food Chain Feature) List-II (Ecological Description)
A. Origin of Grazing Food Chain I. Begins with dead organic matter degraded by saprotrophs
B. Origin of Detritus Food Chain II. Initiates directly with living photosynthetic green plants
C. Dominant conduit in aquatic ecosystems III. Detritus food chain conducts the larger fraction of total energy flow
D. Dominant conduit in terrestrial ecosystems IV. Grazing food chain serves as the major conduit for energy flow

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the source of the grazing food chain.
The grazing food chain (GFC) begins directly with autotrophic living plants capturing solar energy, which is subsequently passed to herbivores and carnivores.

Step 2: Identify the source of the detritus food chain.
The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter (detritus), which is decomposed by heterotrophic saprotrophic fungi and bacteria.

Step 3: Identify the major conduit of energy flow in aquatic systems.
In open water and marine ecosystems, primary producers are consumed rapidly by pelagic herbivores, making the grazing food chain the predominant conduit of energy transfer.

Step 4: Identify the major conduit of energy flow in terrestrial systems.
In forests and grasslands, a substantial portion of plant biomass is not eaten live but falls as litter, resulting in a much larger fraction of energy flowing through the detritus food chain than through the grazing food chain.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Origin of Grazing Food Chain matches initiating directly with living photosynthetic green plants; Origin of Detritus Food Chain matches beginning with dead organic matter degraded by saprotrophs; Dominant conduit in aquatic ecosystems matches the grazing food chain; and Dominant conduit in terrestrial ecosystems matches the detritus food chain conducting the larger fraction of energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q08 - Solar radiation capture and biosphere productivity proportions

questiontext.text:
Match the quantitative ecological parameters in List-I with their accurate values or percentages in List-II:

List-I (Ecological Parameter) List-II (Quantitative Value / Proportion)
A. Fraction of incident solar radiation that is PAR I. Approximately 70 per cent
B. Proportion of PAR captured by plants to sustain the living world II. Less than 50 per cent
C. Surface area of the globe covered by oceans III. Approximately 170 billion tons dry weight
D. Total annual net primary productivity of the entire biosphere IV. 2 to 10 per cent

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the proportion of solar radiation that is PAR.
Of the total incident solar radiation striking the Earth's atmosphere, less than 50 percent falls within the waveband of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).

Step 2: Determine photosynthetic efficiency on PAR.
Autotrophs capture only 2 to 10 percent of the incident PAR, and this fraction sustains the organic energy demands of the living biosphere.

Step 3: Recall the ocean surface coverage.
Oceans occupy approximately 70 percent of Earth's total surface area.

Step 4: Recall global annual net primary productivity.
The total annual net primary productivity of the entire biosphere is estimated to be approximately 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter, with land contributing 115 billion tons and oceans contributing 55 billion tons.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Fraction of incident solar radiation that is PAR matches less than 50 per cent; Proportion of PAR captured by plants matches 2 to 10 per cent; Surface area covered by oceans matches approximately 70 per cent; and Total annual net primary productivity of the entire biosphere matches approximately 170 billion tons dry weight.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q09 - Quantitative trophic data from ecological pyramid models

questiontext.text:
Match the trophic level parameters depicted in standard ecological pyramid models in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II:

List-I (Pyramid Parameter) List-II (Quantitative Value)
A. Number of primary producers in a model grassland pyramid I. \(5,842,000\) individuals
B. Standing biomass of primary producers in an upright terrestrial pyramid II. \(809\text{ kg m}^{-2}\)
C. Standing biomass of primary consumers in an inverted oceanic pyramid III. \(21\text{ g m}^{-2}\)
D. Energy assimilated into primary producers from \(1,000,000\text{ J}\) of incident sunlight IV. \(10,000\text{ J}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Quantify the producers in the grassland number pyramid.
In the grassland pyramid of numbers, a base of \(5,842,000\) primary producers supports \(708,000\) primary consumers, \(354,000\) secondary consumers, and \(3\) top carnivores.

Step 2: Quantify the producer standing crop in the terrestrial biomass pyramid.
In an upright terrestrial biomass pyramid, the primary producers account for a standing dry weight biomass of \(809\text{ kg m}^{-2}\), declining progressively through \(37\text{ kg m}^{-2}\), \(11\text{ kg m}^{-2}\), and \(1.5\text{ kg m}^{-2}\).

Step 3: Quantify the primary consumer biomass in the marine pyramid.
In the inverted biomass pyramid of an aquatic ecosystem, a phytoplankton producer biomass of \(4\text{ g m}^{-2}\) supports a standing zooplankton primary consumer biomass of \(21\text{ g m}^{-2}\).

Step 4: Calculate the energy conversion by primary producers.
Primary producers convert approximately 1 percent of the total available incident solar energy into net primary productivity; hence, from \(1,000,000\text{ J}\) of incident sunlight, primary producers fix \(10,000\text{ J}\) of energy.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Number of primary producers in a grassland pyramid matches \(5,842,000\) individuals; Standing biomass of primary producers in an upright terrestrial pyramid matches \(809\text{ kg m}^{-2}\); Standing biomass of primary consumers in an inverted oceanic pyramid matches \(21\text{ g m}^{-2}\); and Energy assimilated into primary producers from \(1,000,000\text{ J}\) sunlight matches \(10,000\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MCQ_Q10 - Structural features and soil transformation stages

questiontext.text:
Match the structural attributes and soil organic transformations in List-I with their appropriate descriptions in List-II:

List-I (Attribute / Stage) List-II (Description)
A. Stratification I. Total living biomass or count present at a specific trophic level at a particular time
B. Standing crop II. Vertical distribution of different species occupying different physical strata or layers
C. Humus formation III. Breakdown of colloidal organic matter releasing free inorganic nutrients back to soil
D. Mineralisation IV. Accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous colloidal reservoir of nutrients resistant to microbes

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand vertical community architecture.
Stratification refers to the vertical distribution of distinct species occupying different vertical levels in an ecosystem, such as trees in the top canopy, shrubs in the middle stratum, and herbs at the forest floor.

Step 2: Understand the biomass of living material at a trophic tier.
The standing crop is the mass of living organisms (biomass, measured preferably as dry weight) or the total number present in a unit area at a particular time within a trophic level.

Step 3: Understand the nature of humus.
Humus formation leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous colloidal substance that degrades extremely slowly and acts as an important reservoir of soil nutrients.

Step 4: Understand the final release of inorganic nutrients.
Mineralisation is the terminal step of decomposition where specialized microbes degrade humus to liberate essential water-soluble inorganic mineral ions for autotrophic reuse.

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Stratification matches vertical distribution of different species occupying different physical strata; Standing crop matches total living biomass or count present at a specific trophic level at a particular time; Humus formation matches accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous colloidal reservoir of nutrients; and Mineralisation matches breakdown of colloidal organic matter releasing free inorganic nutrients back to the soil.
